summary: Kyrgyzstan is one of Central Asia's easiest destinations to enter: around 60 nationalities — including the whole EU, the UK and the US — stay visa-free for up to 60 days, CIS citizens enter freely, and most other travelers can apply through the official eVisa portal.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Kyrgyz Republic

passportValidity.text: Carry a passport valid for at least 6 months on arrival. The rule airlines and border posts apply in practice; confirm edge cases with a Kyrgyz embassy.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Kyrgyz Republic

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not an entry requirement, but Kyrgyzstan's mountains have minimal rescue infrastructure. A policy covering trekking at altitude and helicopter evacuation is strongly recommended.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Kyrgyz Republic

onwardTicket.text: No formal requirement; border officers rarely ask, but airlines may want to see an onward booking before a one-way flight.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Kyrgyz Republic

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published; visitors may occasionally be asked to show means of support for the stay.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Kyrgyz Republic

currencyLimits.text: Cash of US$10,000 or more (or the equivalent) must be declared under Eurasian Economic Union rules.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Kyrgyz Republic

notes: Standard EAEU duty-free allowances apply for alcohol and tobacco. Confirm current limits before travel.

payments.text: Cards work in Bishkek and Osh supermarkets, hotels and some restaurants, but the country runs on cash. Carry som for guesthouses, yurt camps, marshrutkas and markets, and exchange crisp dollars or euros at bank offices.

safety.text: Kyrgyzstan is generally safe and hospitable; the main risks are practical — rough mountain roads, altitude and occasional petty crime in cities. Sections of the border with Tajikistan have seen periodic tension, so check conditions before traveling to remote border districts.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Kyrgyz Republic Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: June–September is the window for trekking, Song-Kul and the high passes; many mountain roads and yurt camps close outside summer, while the Issyk-Kul beaches peak in July and August.

idp.text: Kyrgyzstan is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Vienna, 1968), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3); Convention on Road Traffic, Vienna, 8 November 1968 (UNTS vol. 1042, p. 17)

driving.text: Kyrgyzstan is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Kyrgyzstan yet.

tips.text: Bring undamaged US dollar or euro notes to exchange — Bishkek exchange offices give fair rates, while ATMs can be scarce and cash-limited outside the two big cities.
Most visa-free visitors need no migration registration for short stays, but some nationalities and long-stayers still do. Check the rules for your passport on arrival or with your guesthouse.
Mountain rescue capacity is minimal — do not trek at altitude without insurance that covers helicopter evacuation, and leave your route with someone before multi-day hikes.
Some areas near the Chinese and Tajik borders require special border-zone permits arranged in advance through tour agencies. Check before planning treks in remote ranges.
Shared taxis and marshrutkas link most towns cheaply; in Bishkek use the Yandex Go app rather than hailing cabs on the street.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Kyrgyzstan?
faq.answer: Probably not for a holiday: around 60 nationalities — including all EU states, the UK, US, Canada, Australia, Japan and the Gulf states — enter visa-free for up to 60 days, and CIS citizens enter freely. Most other travelers can apply online for an eVisa; only the remainder need an embassy visa.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Kyrgyzstan visa-free?
faq.answer: The visa-free allowance for the main list of nationalities is up to 60 days per visit. Leaving and re-entering starts a new period in practice, but frequent back-to-back runs can draw questions — for longer stays look into a visa or residence permit.

faq.question: How does the Kyrgyzstan eVisa work?
faq.answer: Apply online at evisa.e-gov.kg with a passport scan and photo; the tourist eVisa is typically processed in under a week for a fee around US$50 and allows a stay of up to 30 days. Use an international airport or major land crossing, and carry a printout — remote checkpoints may want to see it.

faq.question: Do I need to register with the police in Kyrgyzstan?
faq.answer: Visitors from the 60-day visa-free list are exempt from migration registration for the length of their stay. Some other nationalities and anyone staying long-term may still need to register. Confirm the rule for your passport with your hotel or the local migration office.

faq.question: Is Kyrgyzstan safe for trekking?
faq.answer: Yes, with preparation. Crime against trekkers is rare; the hazards are altitude, weather and remoteness — rescue services are minimal, so carry insurance with helicopter evacuation, hire local guides for high routes, and check conditions for border areas near Tajikistan and China, some of which need permits.
